---
title: "Benchmarking Independent Numerical Backends"
subtitle: "Measure one declared SCNSim task and inspect its retained evidence"
---

**Status:** `CONVERGING`. `run.benchmark()` is an experimental candidate for
independent Julia/JAX execution. It does not change the existing Julia
contracts of `solve()`, `evaluate()`, `optimize()`, or `resolve()`. This guide
describes the candidate API and its current limits; it does not claim numerical
or performance results.

## Declare one task

Build the physical `CircuitPlan`, select the original or a derived View, and
declare the same typed Direct, root, response, or Optimization Spec used by the
existing analysis operations. The benchmark records the exact Plan, View, Spec,
effective parameter input, backend identities, and outputs for that request.

```python
from pathlib import Path

from scnsim import BenchmarkSpec

record = run.benchmark(
    root_view,
    root_spec,
    workspace=Path("workspaces/benchmark/chapter-02-root"),
    benchmark=BenchmarkSpec(device="cpu", cpu_threads=(1, 32)),
)
```

The default request is one complete sample for each declared CPU arm and
thread profile. A repeat is a new task with its own sample identity and fresh
workspace. The CPU arms are the original whole-Julia task, common Python-host
Julia factorization reuse, common Python-host pivoted LU, and the independent
Python-host JAX backend. To reproduce native Julia thread configurations under
the same physical quota, declare them explicitly:

```python
BenchmarkSpec(cpu_threads=(32,), julia_threads=32, julia_blas_threads=32)
BenchmarkSpec(cpu_threads=(32,), julia_threads=32, julia_blas_threads=1)
```

Use distinct workspaces for these distinct requests. Both fields apply only to
native Julia in the Julia arms; Python host NumPy/BLAS and JAX/XLA still follow
`cpu_threads`. Each omitted field independently defaults to the quota. Requested
and actual native counts remain bound to their task and checkpoint identities;
this comparison introduces no automatic resource tuning or candidate threading.
The JAX arm does not start Julia for discovery,
preflight, lowering, root calculation, optimization, or report composition.
The observations in this case package use CPU devices only and make no
non-CPU device-support claim.

The Optimization path uses the declared seed, sigma, population settings, and
complete-generation budget. The benchmark keeps candidate order, baseline
anchors, checkpoints, and the strict-best winner in its own record. A separate
`cohort` task evaluates one exact ordered list of canonical `ParameterSet`
records on the common Python-host arms. Partial bindings override the declared
effective baseline closure. The cohort and a closed-loop CMA run
are distinct observations. The original whole-Julia control remains a full
optimization task; it is not converted into a forced-CMA cohort.

## Compare mesh policies without changing the Plan

For a transmission line, the current `ElectricalResolution` policy remains the
dynamic-section baseline. A benchmark `MeshSpec` may declare fixed per-line
section counts or ordered parameter groups with fixed counts. Those overrides
belong to the benchmark request, not to the `CircuitPlan`; each task records
the requested policy and the actual compiled N and dx at its evaluated points.

The Chapter 7 position model provides a maintained two-conductor workload: its
line lengths are `x` and `8 mm - x`, it has a 20 fF midpoint shunt and four
terminated 50 Ω signal ports, and its Direct request uses 61 frequencies from
1 to 10 GHz. The declared dynamic policy is compared with the work packet's
full-range fixed and grouped fixed requests at positions 2, 4, and 6 mm and at
the requested neighbors of the 4 mm group boundary. The physical Plan stays
the same. These observations describe discretization and measured differences;
they do not create an S-parameter error bound or an automatic mesh default.

## Read the observations

The returned `BenchmarkResult` is an immutable view of one benchmark record.
`to_json()` returns its canonical manifest; `to_html()` renders that same
record without starting a calculation, choosing a latest result, or mutating
the task evidence. A record may contain completed, failed, interrupted, or
pending tasks. Any recorded report status remains separate, so report handling
does not change a numerical outcome.

The HTML gives a compact, 12-significant-digit summary of recorded evaluation
values and includes the event data in disclosure sections. The canonical JSON
manifest remains the exact tagged-value and identity authority.
Original Julia observations are decoded post hoc from the verified native
result and retained baseline/generation artifacts. Their native order and
source references remain explicit; they do not supply per-evaluation timings.
Interrupted or failed tasks can show the actual retained numerical records
without claiming a terminal result artifact or winner.
Native parameter sweeps show the actual ordered point values, statuses and
payload/chunk references. Partial post-stop rows refer to the retained verified
point checkpoints; Direct arrays retain their existing units and axes.
Their source catalogs retain the producer's artifact paths even when decoding
reads from a localized point directory. A secondary post hoc decoding error is
recorded as `numerical_observation_error`; it does not replace the original
native terminal failure.

Measurements retain monotonic start and duration, work counts, memory
observations, and details. Each new row binds its invocation clock ID, source,
unit and monotonic origin; `start_ns` is relative to that row's origin.
Historical rows retain their recorded legacy root clock binding. The report
labels missing per-row clocks explicitly and does not infer origins or compare
start positions across invocation clocks. The global `benchmark_end_to_end` interval covers
shared preparation and the serial benchmark arms. A task's `end_to_end` interval
covers that task's arm-specific request and binding preparation through
completion. Stage intervals can overlap; the report presents each interval
separately and does not add stages into a total. Startup, initialization, first
JIT compilation, later evaluations, transfers, solving, committing, decoding,
and report rendering remain distinguishable when observed. `new_shape` means
first executable-signature preparation, whose numerical tensor shapes/dtypes,
job kind, family, Port realizability and batch size are distinct from node IDs
and lineage. It does not prove uncached machine-code generation or a changed
matrix dimension. A numerical batch's timing is attached to each result;
comparisons must count that batch once.
Common-host Julia observations expose the exact `batch_id`,
`backend_invocation_start_ns`, `batch_transfer_and_compute_start_ns` and
`batch_transfer_and_compute_end_ns` copied from the same measured interval.
Use the invocation identity with the batch ID to deduplicate its repeated
result evidence; the interval includes transfer and compute and is not a
separate timer for every job.

The optional progress callback receives a frozen `TaskEvent` after its
observation is durable. Native original Optimization uses `progress` events;
Python population generations start at 1 and its baseline is generation0.
Benchmark preserves the callback's original exception and `KeyboardInterrupt`,
retaining partial observations. This does not change the ordinary `optimize()`
callback wrapper.

Standalone root tasks first evaluate and acknowledge a sealed baseline-root
record, then continue each requested nonbaseline point independently from that
anchor. They reuse the actual baseline or duplicate-point results and preserve
requested order. This root-anchor record is not a CMA resume checkpoint;
`resume_from` remains restricted to full Optimization.

Target values for this experiment are collected from actual Julia Results at
the exact declared parameters and Views before backend comparisons. The
private case manifest records each source Result identity, selector, unit,
value, and numerical input request hash alongside the public benchmark record.
The public benchmark declaration binds the target value in its objective spec;
common-host and JAX outcomes use benchmark task identities and artifacts, not
borrowed Julia Result identities. Candidate-cohort records preserve ordered
input ParameterSets and per-candidate outcomes, separately from
complete-generation optimization records.

```python
print(record.to_json())
html = record.to_html()
```

Use a browser to inspect the returned HTML when reviewing figures or tables.
Source inspection and successful serialization alone do not establish that the
rendered report is visually usable. Keep the original manifest and linked
artifacts with the report so each displayed observation retains its provenance.

## Scope and interpretation

The current candidate supports Direct S/Y/Z requests, diagonal roots, scalar
response elements, and Optimization expressions built from those quantities.
HB and other quantity families fail explicitly. Arrays use Float64 and
Complex128. The observations in this guide execute CPU tasks only. The
maintained examples provide one-conductor and two-conductor line cases; there
is no maintained physical input with more than two conductors, so this workflow
does not invent one.

Performance and numerical observations have no automatic acceptance threshold
or error tolerance. The report can show timings, work counts, output values,
mesh refinement, and failed or partial tasks, but it does not declare a backend
winner or a design target met. Interpretation remains specific to the recorded
inputs, algorithms, environment, and execution identities.
